title: Book 02 — Chapter 6, Session 1: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 6: The Issue of Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Questions were checked against the original Session 1 source. Political motives are presented as competing hypotheses; the forced journey and the source's stated historical facts are distinguished from those hypotheses.

revision_policy: Preserve Session 1 as a separate learning and assessment unit from Session 2.
Distinguish historical facts from hypotheses about Ma’mun’s and Fadl ibn Sahl’s motives.
Use cross-sectarian historical citations without claiming that they settle every disputed motive.
Do not treat Ma’mun’s intellectual interests as proof of political sincerity.

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What historical issue does Mutahhari examine in Session 1, and why does he say the terminology of ‘heir’ or ‘crown prince’ needs historical care?
questions.answer: Mutahhari examines the appointment of Imam al-Rida as Ma’mun’s crown prince. He notes that terms such as “heir” and “crown prince” are historically situated expressions and were not used in the same way at the beginning of Islam. The practice of a caliph designating a successor and taking allegiance for that successor first appeared in the Umayyad period when Mu‘awiyah designated Yazid. Mutahhari therefore uses the familiar historical label while reminding readers that the terminology and political institution developed over time. This context matters because the appointment of Imam al-Rida should be understood as part of a later political practice, not as an institution that had always existed in the same form.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why was Imam al-Rida made crown prince?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Which earlier ruler first introduced the practice of appointing a successor during his own lifetime, according to Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies Mu‘awiyah’s designation of his son Yazid as the first introduction of the practice of a caliph appointing a successor during his lifetime and taking allegiance for him. He notes that the terminology “crown prince” was not necessarily used at that time, but the political practice was established. This historical precedent is important because the appointment of Imam al-Rida took place within a political system in which dynastic succession had already become a feature of caliphal rule.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why was Imam al-Rida made crown prince?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What common criticism do some people make of the decisions of Imam al-Hasan and Imam al-Rida, as described by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that critics sometimes treat the two situations as parallel compromises with an unjust caliphate. They argue that Imam al-Hasan should not have handed over the affairs of government and should have fought until martyrdom, while Imam al-Rida should not have accepted the crown-prince position and should also have resisted until death. The criticism assumes that in both cases the Imam reached an agreement with a ruler who had taken power unjustly. Mutahhari raises the question to examine the historical circumstances and the reasoning behind the decisions rather than assuming that the two situations were identical.
questions.source_locator: Opening question — Why was Imam al-Rida made crown prince?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari describe the general attitude of the Abbasid rulers toward the Alawis?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes the Abbasid attitude toward the Alawis as marked by persistent hostility, persecution, imprisonment, and killing. He says that from the beginning of Abbasid rule, the dynasty pursued the Alawis and sought to suppress their political influence. The tragedy of Karbala under the Umayyads made the persecution of the Ahl al-Bayt especially prominent in public memory, but Mutahhari argues that the Abbasids also committed severe crimes against the descendants of the Prophet. This history provides the political background for understanding why Ma’mun’s decision to bring Imam al-Rida into the succession was surprising and difficult to interpret.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasid attitude towards the Alawis

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What example does Mutahhari give of Mansur’s treatment of the descendants of Imam al-Hasan?
questions.answer: Mutahhari recounts that Mansur killed many descendants of Imam al-Hasan, including people to whom he had previously given allegiance, and confined a large group of them in extremely harsh prisons. He describes prisoners being denied water, bread, and even permission to leave their cells to relieve themselves. At times, Mansur allegedly ordered the prison roof to be brought down upon them. Mutahhari uses this example to demonstrate the severity of Abbasid persecution and to show that the dynasty’s hostility toward the Alawis was not limited to political disagreement or occasional imprisonment.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasid attitude towards the Alawis

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What examples does Mutahhari give to show that Abbasid rulers were ruthless even toward members of their own political circle?
questions.answer: Mutahhari mentions the killing of Abu Muslim after he had served the Abbasids, the destruction of the Barmakid family despite its long service to Harun, and the violent conflict between Ma’mun and his brother Amin. These examples show that Abbasid rulers were prepared to eliminate even powerful allies or relatives when they became obstacles to political control. Mutahhari uses this pattern to caution readers against assuming that Ma’mun’s intellectual abilities or apparent respect for the Ahl al-Bayt automatically reveal his political intentions.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasid attitude towards the Alawis

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Which non-Shi‘ah historical source does Mutahhari use when discussing Imam al-Rida’s succession, and who wrote it?
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites Maqatil al-Talibiyyin, written by Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani. He identifies the author as a non-Shi‘ah historian of Umayyad background and emphasizes that the work is a historical account of the deaths and rebellions of the descendants of Abu Talib. The book devotes a substantial section to Imam al-Rida’s succession. Mutahhari uses it to show that the account of the appointment is not based only on Shi‘ah historical sources or on Shi‘ah emotional attachment to the Imams.
questions.source_locator: The issue of Imam al-Rida’s succession and historical citations

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari compare Maqatil al-Talibiyyin with Shaykh Mufid’s al-Irshad?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that he compared the account of Imam al-Rida’s succession in Maqatil al-Talibiyyin with the material in Shaykh Mufid’s al-Irshad. He found the accounts very similar, almost as though both had drawn on the same underlying historical evidence. This comparison strengthens his point that the narrative is not confined to one sectarian source tradition. It does not mean that every historical question is settled, but it gives Mutahhari reason to use both Shi‘ah and non-Shi‘ah historical material in examining the event.
questions.source_locator: The issue of Imam al-Rida’s succession and historical citations

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari describe Ma’mun’s intellectual reputation, and why is that relevant to the crown-prince question?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes Ma’mun as exceptionally knowledgeable and interested in scholarship, philosophy, hadith, history, logic, literature, medicine, and other sciences. He also mentions Ma’mun’s participation in debates about the caliphate and his willingness to convene scholarly discussions. This intellectual reputation makes the crown-prince episode more complex: Ma’mun cannot be understood simply as an ignorant or impulsive ruler. Mutahhari nevertheless distinguishes intellectual ability and interest in Shi‘ism from political conduct. A ruler may admire the Ahl al-Bayt or value their knowledge while still acting against their interests when his power is threatened.
questions.source_locator: Ma’mun and the Shi‘ism

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What story does Mutahhari relate about Harun al-Rashid’s attitude toward Imam Musa al-Kazim and his own son?
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites a report in which Ma’mun says that he learned his respect for Shi‘ism from his father Harun. When Ma’mun asked Harun why he treated Imam Musa al-Kazim harshly despite his apparent reverence for him, Harun replied with the proverb that “kingdom is sterile.” He explained that political power can override family affection: even if his own son challenged him for the caliphate, he would be willing to kill him. Mutahhari uses the story to illustrate the contradiction between personal or intellectual admiration for a religious figure and the ruthless demands of political rule.
questions.source_locator: Ma’mun and the Shi‘ism — Intellectual sympathy versus political conduct

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What is the explanation attributed to Shaykh Saduq and Shaykh Mufid for Ma’mun’s initial proposal to Imam al-Rida?
questions.answer: Shaykh Saduq, and apparently Shaykh Mufid, accepted the possibility that Ma’mun initially intended sincerely to return the caliphate to its rightful owners. According to the story, during his conflict with his brother Amin, Ma’mun feared defeat and made a vow to God that if he were granted victory, he would return the caliphate to the Ahl al-Bayt. After he became victorious, he proposed the transfer to Imam al-Rida. Mutahhari presents this as one historical explanation, not as an established fact, and says that even if Ma’mun began sincerely, his intentions did not remain the same until the end.
questions.source_locator: The views of Shaykh Mufid and Shaykh Saduq

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What uncertainty surrounds the theory that Fadl ibn Sahl initiated the appointment of Imam al-Rida?
questions.answer: One theory is that Fadl ibn Sahl, Ma’mun’s powerful minister, initiated the proposal and persuaded Ma’mun to appoint Imam al-Rida. Mutahhari notes that some historians considered Fadl a Shi‘ah who sincerely wanted to transfer authority to the Alawis. However, the evidence for this claim is not decisive, and the Imam’s own opposition to Fadl makes the theory difficult to accept without qualification. Mutahhari also raises the possibility that Fadl had political motives that were not in the interests of Islam. He repeatedly emphasizes that the origin and purpose of the initiative remain uncertain and should not be presented as settled history.
questions.source_locator: The second probability — Did Fadl ibn Sahl initiate the appointment?

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What were the possible political aims behind Ma’mun’s appointment of Imam al-Rida that Mutahhari discusses?
questions.answer: Mutahhari outlines several possible aims. Ma’mun may have wanted to attract Iranian support by appearing to satisfy their affection for the Ahl al-Bayt. He may have sought to calm Alawi revolts by bringing their most respected figure into the government, thereby weakening the motivation for rebellion. He may also have wanted to disarm Imam al-Rida himself: once the Imam held a government title, dissatisfied people might blame him for the regime’s failures rather than criticize the Abbasids. Mutahhari stresses that these are explanations proposed by historians and analysts, not facts that can be established with complete certainty.
questions.source_locator: The third probability — Attracting Iranian support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Why might Ma’mun have wanted to attract Iranian support by appointing Imam al-Rida?
questions.answer: Mutahhari notes that many Iranians had strong affection for the Ahl al-Bayt and that Alawi movements had repeatedly arisen against Abbasid rule. By appointing Imam al-Rida as crown prince, Ma’mun could present himself as satisfying a long-standing Iranian desire for leadership from the Prophet’s family. The source also says that Ma’mun gave the Imam the title al-Rida in this context, presenting it as a political gesture intended to win support. Mutahhari treats this as one possible explanation for Ma’mun’s policy, not as a motive proven beyond doubt.
questions.source_locator: The third probability — Attracting Iranian support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How could appointing Imam al-Rida as crown prince have weakened Alawi rebellions, according to one hypothesis discussed by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari suggests that Ma’mun may have hoped to neutralize Alawi opposition by bringing its most respected representative into the government. If Imam al-Rida became crown prince, supporters of the Alawis might hesitate to rebel because they could be told that their leader already had a share in the government. The appointment could therefore weaken the unity and motivation of Alawi movements without requiring the Abbasids to defeat each rebellion militarily. Mutahhari presents this as a possible political strategy aimed at disarming the Alawis and reducing the threat they posed to Abbasid rule.
questions.source_locator: The third probability — Neutralizing Alawi rebellions

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari mean by the hypothesis that Ma’mun wanted to ‘disarm’ Imam al-Rida by giving him a government position?
questions.answer: The hypothesis is that Ma’mun wanted to bring Imam al-Rida into the political system so that the Imam could no longer criticize the Abbasid government from a position of independence. If the Imam accepted a title but could not change the system, people might become disappointed with him and blame him for the regime’s failures. The appointment could also allow Ma’mun to claim that the Alawis had been given a share in government and therefore had no reason to oppose him. Mutahhari explains this as a possible method of weakening a popular critic by making him appear responsible for the system he had previously criticized.
questions.source_locator: The third probability — Disarming Imam al-Rida’s opposition

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What route was chosen for Imam al-Rida’s journey from Medina to Marw, and why was Kufa avoided?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the authorities selected a route through Basra and Khuzistan toward Nishapur, deliberately avoiding Kufa and other places where the Imam could meet significant Shi‘ah populations. The route was chosen before the journey and was intended to prevent the Imam from passing through areas where followers could gather around him. The Imam and his relatives were brought under surveillance and without being consulted about the journey. The route therefore demonstrates that the transfer was a controlled political operation rather than a voluntary visit or ordinary invitation.
questions.source_locator: The historical facts — The forced journey from Medina to Marw

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Who was Jaludi, and what happened when Imam al-Rida tried to intercede for him?
questions.answer: Jaludi, or Juludi, was the general appointed to escort Imam al-Rida and the group from Medina to Marw. Mutahhari describes him as strongly loyal to Ma’mun and hostile toward the Imam. When Ma’mun asked for opinions about the crown-prince plan, two men openly opposed it and were executed. When Ma’mun turned to Jaludi, Imam al-Rida quietly asked Ma’mun to spare him. Jaludi mistakenly thought the Imam was speaking against him and begged Ma’mun not to accept the Imam’s word. Ma’mun had already promised not to act on the Imam’s request, and Jaludi was executed. The episode illustrates both the hostility surrounding the journey and the Imam’s attempt to protect even someone who opposed him.
questions.source_locator: The historical facts — The forced journey from Medina to Marw

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How did Imam al-Rida initially respond when the crown-prince proposal was presented to him in Marw?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the Imam strongly rejected the proposal. Ma’mun had first brought him to Marw and separated him from the rest of the Hashimite group before raising the issue. When the proposal was presented, the Imam did not accept it as a voluntary or honourable appointment. The historical reports cited by Mutahhari say that the Imam continued to refuse even after the matter was pressed by Ma’mun’s representatives, until the threat of death made refusal impossible. The acceptance must therefore be understood in the context of coercion, not as evidence that the Imam sought the position.
questions.source_locator: Imam al-Rida’s refusal — Rejecting the offer before the threat

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: What threat finally compelled Imam al-Rida to accept the crown-prince position?
questions.answer: According to the reports Mutahhari cites, Ma’mun and his representatives threatened to kill Imam al-Rida if he continued to refuse. They invoked the example of Imam ‘Ali’s participation in the six-member council and argued that he too had accepted a political process despite believing the caliphate was his right. The Imam finally accepted because his life was threatened. Mutahhari emphasizes that the acceptance was not freely chosen and that the question of whether the Imam should have sacrificed his life rather than accept the title is a separate moral issue for readers to consider. The source treats the threat and coerced acceptance as historical facts.
questions.source_locator: Imam al-Rida’s refusal — Acceptance under threat

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Explain the political background that made Ma’mun’s decision to appoint Imam al-Rida as crown prince so difficult to interpret.
questions.answer: Mutahhari places the appointment against a long history of Abbasid hostility toward the Alawis. The Abbasids had imprisoned and killed descendants of the Prophet, and Alawi rebellions continued during the reigns of Harun and Ma’mun. The dynasty also eliminated powerful allies and even members of its own family when they threatened its rule, as seen in the cases of Abu Muslim, the Barmakids, and Ma’mun’s conflict with Amin. Against this background, Ma’mun’s decision to bring Imam al-Rida from Medina and appoint him as crown prince appears surprising. Mutahhari notes that Abbasid political plans were often secret and that even historians could not establish the rulers’ true intentions. The appointment must therefore be examined through both the established historical events and the competing explanations of Ma’mun’s motives.
questions.source_locator: The Abbasid attitude towards the Alawis

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Evaluate the evidence Mutahhari uses to show that the history of Imam al-Rida’s succession is not based exclusively on Shi‘ah sources.
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites Maqatil al-Talibiyyin by Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, whom he identifies as a non-Shi‘ah historian of Umayyad background. The work records the rebellions and deaths of the descendants of Abu Talib and devotes a substantial section to Imam al-Rida’s succession. Mutahhari compares its account with Shaykh Mufid’s al-Irshad and says that the two are very similar, as though they drew on the same underlying historical evidence. He therefore argues that the historical discussion is supported by material beyond Shi‘ah sources alone. This does not eliminate every uncertainty about Ma’mun’s motives, but it gives a wider evidential basis for the main events. In an examination answer, distinguish cross-source corroboration of events from certainty about the private intentions of political actors.
questions.source_locator: The issue of Imam al-Rida’s succession and historical citations

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari reconcile Ma’mun’s apparent respect for Shi‘ism and scholarship with his political treatment of Imam al-Rida?
questions.answer: Mutahhari acknowledges that Ma’mun was highly learned, intellectually curious, and interested in Shi‘ism. He refers to reports of Ma’mun debating the caliphate with Sunni scholars and discussing the status of Imam ‘Ali. He also recounts Ma’mun’s statement that he learned his respect for Shi‘ism from his father Harun, who revered Imam Musa al-Kazim while still treating him harshly. The proverb “kingdom is sterile” explains the contradiction: political power can override personal affection, intellectual admiration, and even family bonds. A ruler may respect the knowledge or spiritual standing of an Imam but still act against him when the Imam’s authority threatens the ruler’s control. Mutahhari therefore warns against inferring Ma’mun’s political intentions solely from his intellectual interests or apparent religious sympathies.
questions.source_locator: Ma’mun and the Shi‘ism

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Compare the three main political explanations Mutahhari discusses for Ma’mun’s appointment of Imam al-Rida.
questions.answer: Mutahhari discusses three broad possibilities. First, Ma’mun may initially have acted sincerely because of a vow he made during his conflict with Amin to return the caliphate to the Ahl al-Bayt if God granted him victory; this is the view associated with Shaykh Saduq and apparently Shaykh Mufid, although Mutahhari says Ma’mun’s intentions later changed. Second, Fadl ibn Sahl may have initiated the appointment, either from sincere Shi‘ah motives or for a more dangerous political purpose; Mutahhari treats this as uncertain and questions the claim that Fadl was sincere. Third, Ma’mun himself may have initiated the appointment as a political strategy: to attract Iranian support, neutralize Alawi rebellions, or disarm Imam al-Rida by drawing him into the government. Mutahhari does not present these hypotheses as established facts. He stresses that the Abbasids concealed their political plans and that the evidence does not permit certainty about every motive.
questions.source_locator: The third probability — Attracting Iranian support

questions.unit_title: Chapter 6: Imam al-Rida as the Crown Prince (Session 1)
questions.prompt: Describe the forced journey of Imam al-Rida to Marw and explain what the details reveal about the nature of the appointment.
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that Ma’mun summoned Imam al-Rida from Medina without prior consultation or an explanation of the purpose. A large group of the Imam’s relatives was also brought under surveillance and against their free will. The route was deliberately selected to avoid Shi‘ah centres: the Imam was not to pass through Kufa but was taken through Basra and Khuzistan toward Nishapur. The escort was chosen from people loyal to Ma’mun and hostile to the Imam. Jaludi, the appointed general, was so opposed to the plan that he openly disagreed with Ma’mun, and two other opponents were executed. When the Imam tried to intercede for Jaludi, Jaludi misunderstood his words and was still executed. The Imam and his relatives arrived in Marw under surveillance and effectively under arrest. These details show that the appointment was imposed through state power and controlled movement, not negotiated as a voluntary political partnership.
questions.source_locator: The historical facts — The forced journey from Medina to Marw
